sections.h2: Where is Holladay, Utah, and what kind of city is it?
sections.html:
Holladay is a city in the middle of Salt Lake County, wedged between Murray, Millcreek and Cottonwood Heights, with its eastern edge against the Wasatch National Forest. It covers 8.50 square miles, all of it land, and sits at about 4,465 feet above sea level.

The city is almost entirely residential. Three ZIP codes cover it (84117, 84121 and 84124), so a Holladay address can carry a different mailing ZIP than the neighbor two streets over. Sellers should check which one appears on the county parcel record before they sign anything.

Only about 4.5% of Holladay homes sat empty at the 2020 count, so few houses in the city were standing vacant when the Census Bureau counted.

sections.h2: How did Holladay start, and why does its history matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Holladay began in 1847, when pioneers from the Mississippi Company, including John Holladay of Alabama, reached the Salt Lake Valley and found a spring-fed stream they called Spring Creek near what is now Kentucky Avenue. A few men wintered in dugouts there, and the settlement took Holladay's name.

The area later went by Big Cottonwood and then Holladay-Cottonwood. The city was incorporated on November 29, 1999 as Holladay-Cottonwood. The name was shortened to Holladay on December 14, 1999. Holladay claims to be the oldest continuously inhabited settlement in Utah, a claim that rests on Salt Lake City being briefly abandoned in 1857.

For a seller, the age of the settlement is a reminder that the city itself is only a few decades old. Holladay was a county community before 1999, and a house that was remodeled in that earlier period can have a permit history worth checking at the Holladay building office before a buyer asks.

  • Ask the building office whether an older addition or basement finish has a closed permit.
  • The city has grown through four annexations, including ones in 2002 and 2015, so a few parcels joined Holladay after they were built.
  • Lot lines in older subdivisions sometimes differ from fences, so a survey from a state-certified surveyor settles it. The city does not mark property lines itself.

sections.h2: What happened to the old Cottonwood Mall site?
sections.html:
The Cottonwood Mall opened in 1962 as the first large indoor shopping mall in Utah and closed in 2007. The Holladay council declared it blighted that August, the buildings came down in mid-2008, and a redevelopment stalled in 2009 when the original developer filed for bankruptcy.

The 56-acre site near 4800 S. Highland Drive is now called Holladay Hills. A Salt Lake Tribune report from October 2024 described a plan for 614 residential units and up to 750,000 square feet of shops, restaurants and offices, with a 147-unit apartment building and a 38-townhome project already underway. Some of the townhomes were listed at $1 million or more.

New construction a few blocks away changes how nearby sellers are compared. A buyer touring a Holladay house built decades ago is often also looking at a new townhome, and the older house has to justify its price on lot, location or condition. If the older home needs work, an as-is sale avoids that comparison altogether.

sections.h2: Which schools and services reach Holladay homes?
sections.html:
The Granite School District serves Holladay, and Olympus High School, which has stood in Holladay since 1953, is the only public high school inside city limits. School assignment follows district boundary maps, so the school attached to an address is worth confirming on the district site rather than assuming from the street name.

Holladay runs under a council-manager form of government, adopted in 2003 after four years under a strong mayor. The Community Development office handles planning and building and can be reached at 801-527-3890. Salt Lake County handles assessment, tax collection and recording.

sections.h2: What permit rules in Holladay can affect a sale?
sections.html:
Holladay requires a building permit for additions, remodels of any size, basement finishes, reroofing, solar, pools, spas and front-yard fencing, and it reviews plans against current codes before it issues one. A Certificate of Occupancy follows the final inspections.

Some work needs no permit. Decks lower than 18 inches above grade, backyard fences up to 6 feet, and like-for-like swaps of plumbing fixtures, lights and receptacles are on the exempt list, along with cabinets, trim, carpet and paint. A detached shed of 200 square feet or less and under 20 feet tall skips the building permit but still gets a zoning check.

  • Removing a tree on public or private property can require a permit under city code sections 13.77.080 and 13.77.090.
  • Front-yard fences top out at 4 feet. Side and rear yards allow 6 feet.
  • If an inspector finds a violation, a Correction Notice generally gives about 30 days to fix it.
  • HOA covenants are enforced by each subdivision's association, not by the city planning office.

An unpermitted basement or addition does not stop a cash sale. It does stop many financed sales, because the appraiser and lender ask what is legal and what is not. Sellers who want to avoid that argument can sell the house in its current state.

sections.h2: What earthquake and soil issues should Holladay sellers know about?
sections.html:
Holladay sits in the Wasatch Front, where the Wasatch fault is Utah's most active fault, and the Utah Geological Survey publishes liquefaction maps for these valleys. The last large earthquake on the Salt Lake City segment was about 1,400 years ago, and large quakes of roughly magnitude 7 have recurred about every 1,300 years.

Liquefaction is most likely in low central parts of a valley with shallow groundwater, so risk varies from one lot to the next. The survey also says the maps show only general patterns and that a site-specific study by a Utah-licensed engineer and geologist is needed for a particular lot.

Older masonry is the main concern. Unreinforced brick buildings from roughly the 1920s to the 1960s were not designed for sideways ground motion. Sellers of Holladay brick houses from that era should expect buyers to ask about bracing and chimney anchors.

sections.h2: How do property tax dates work for a Holladay house?
sections.html:
Salt Lake County bills Holladay property tax, and the full year is due November 30 with delinquency starting December 1. Valuation notices go out in July and August, tax notices are mailed by November 1, and the property is valued as of January 1.

StepTimingNote
Value set as ofJanuary 1Lien date for the year
Valuation notices mailedJuly and AugustShows the assessed value
Appeal window (2026)July 31 to September 15Board of Equalization
Tax notices mailedBy November 1Treasurer collects
Last day without penaltyNovember 30Delinquent December 1

The appeal board reviews only the current year's market value, and an appeal needs evidence such as a recent purchase, an appraisal, or at least three comparable sales. The Treasurer's office, at 385-468-8300, also takes applications for tax relief programs. Details are on the Salt Lake County tax administration page.

A home that was the owner's main residence is taxed on 55% of market value through Utah's primary residential exemption, which takes 45% off. After a sale, the new owner has to file a fresh claim with the county, and a missed claim can mean tax on the full value for that year. Sellers who rented the house out should expect a declaration process as well.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale close in Holladay, and what gets recorded?
sections.html:
A cash sale in Holladay closes through a title or escrow company, and the deed is recorded with the Salt Lake County Recorder. With no lender involved, there is no appraisal contingency or loan approval to wait on.

The county's published recording requirements show what a clean deed needs. The Recorder charges a flat $40 per recording as of the October 2024 schedule, and the document must carry a Salt Lake County legal description, the parcel number, an original notarized signature and the buyer's mailing address. The office does not prepare, notarize or supply forms, and it mails originals back about two to three weeks after imaging. Questions go to 385-468-8145.

  • Order a title search early if the house came through a family trust or an estate.
  • Confirm the names on the deed match the names on the signature page and the notary block.
  • Ask the title officer to prorate the year's tax between you and the buyer at closing.

sections.h2: What choices do Holladay sellers have?
sections.html:
A Holladay owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer. Listing usually means cleaning, repairs and showings in a market where new townhomes compete, while a cash offer buys the house as it stands.

  • Inherited houses with deferred maintenance, often in the older parts of the city.
  • Rentals with tenants in place, where showings are hard to schedule.
  • Homes with basement or addition work that was never permitted.
  • Owners behind on payments who need a closing date they can count on.

Compare any offer against what a listing would net after repairs, commission and carrying costs, and ask for the closing date and the buyer's proof of funds in writing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Holladay house with an unpermitted basement?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase the house in its current state, though the lack of a permit may lower what a buyer will pay. Financed buyers and their appraisers often object, so listing the house may require closing out the work first through the Holladay building office.

faqs.q: When is property tax due on a Holladay home?
faqs.a: November 30 each year, billed by the Salt Lake County Treasurer. Taxes become delinquent on December 1. If you sell mid-year, the title company normally prorates the bill at closing.

faqs.q: Does the new owner keep my primary residential exemption?
faqs.a: No. The exemption does not pass to a buyer automatically. The new owner files an application with the county, and a missed filing can mean tax on the full market value for that year.

faqs.q: How long does recording the deed take in Salt Lake County?
faqs.a: Recording is usually handled by the title company right after closing. The county returns original documents by mail about two to three weeks after they are imaged.

faqs.q: Is Holladay in a liquefaction or fault zone?
faqs.a: That depends on the lot. The Utah Geological Survey publishes liquefaction and fault maps for the Wasatch Front, and it recommends a site-specific study by a Utah-licensed professional for any particular property.
